controls.description: Total central excise per litre on petrol and diesel, summed. The discretionary buffer between a crude move and a consumer price.

gaps.reason: At least three changes fall in this window — a Budget 2019 increase, a March 2020 increase, and the May 2020 increase of about Rs 10 on petrol and Rs 13 on diesel — and no retrievable primary document states the resulting levels. That they happened is not in doubt: the level entering the window is Rs 17.98 and PRS Legislative Research reports Rs 32.9 on petrol and Rs 31.8 on diesel for October 2021, so the rate roughly doubled inside it. Holding the 2018 level across the largest fuel-tax increase in the sample would put a fabricated constant into the one control that exists to absorb discretionary tax moves, so the window is declared unknown and the months in it drop out of the controlled regression.

links.description: Crude into the import bill and through to consumer prices. This is the link the fuel-tax buffer sits inside: excise and state VAT are adjusted by hand, in the opposite direction, precisely when crude moves, so an uncontrolled estimate here measures a fiscal decision as if it were a pricing mechanism.

Inflation into the policy response, measured on the money-market rate rather than on the repo rate itself. That is a deliberate weakening of the claim: the corridor's transmission is what is observable in a free monthly series, and calling it the policy rate would assert a passthrough this repository has not measured.

code.note: engine_version is static and identifies nothing on its own; commit is what names the code behind this artifact. dirty=true means tracked files differed from that commit when the run started, so the SHA locates the run but does not fully reproduce it. dirty=null means the run could not tell.

disclaimer: Aurex is a research and education tool. It produces probability distributions, not advice. Short-horizon price direction is not reliably forecastable, and nothing here changes that.

freshness.policy: A blocking series — the price series, and the exchange rate of any published lens — must reach the run date within its declared tolerance or the run publishes nothing and exits non-zero. Tolerances are calendar days and are stated per series with the publication calendar they were derived from. Non-blocking series are measured and reported here but never block: a stale factor moves a fitted loading, which is a smaller problem than a fabricated price.

series.detail: dxy: last observation 2026-08-28 is 7 days behind the run date, tolerance is 10 (US business days, published in arrears)

tolerance.calendar: US business days, published in arrears
tolerance.rationale: DTWEXBGS runs materially further behind than the other FRED series — six days behind on the 2026-07-30 run, which was an ordinary day. Ten days is set from that observed lag rather than from the market calendar; a tighter number would fire on healthy runs and train the reader to ignore it.

series.detail: gpr: last observation 2026-09-01 is 3 days behind the run date, tolerance is 10 (calendar days; the daily file is refreshed every Monday)

tolerance.calendar: calendar days; the daily file is refreshed every Monday
tolerance.rationale: The index itself is daily and covers weekends, but the workbook carrying it is rebuilt weekly — the authors state Monday, moving to the next business day when Monday is a federal holiday. So the last observation sits up to six days behind by Sunday, seven with the holiday shift. Ten days leaves room for one skipped update to be visible without a healthy Saturday run reading as a fault.

series.detail: ibja_gold: last observation 2026-09-04 is 0 days behind the run date, tolerance is 6 (Indian business days)

tolerance.rationale: Not blocking. IBJA closes for local holidays that cluster several days deep, and §0's sixth rule already covers the consequence: where there is no observation the premium is NaN rather than computed. Six days keeps a Diwali week from reading as a fault while still surfacing a dead feed.

series.detail: local_cpi: last observation 2025-03-01 is 552 days behind the run date, tolerance is 45 (monthly, published in arrears)

tolerance.rationale: A monthly index released a few weeks after the month it measures, so 45 days is the ordinary lag rather than a fault. THIS SERIES IS EXPECTED TO READ STALE: the OECD discontinued it upstream and its last observation is 2025-03. That is deliberately not papered over by widening the tolerance to swallow it — the chain is estimated to the last observation the publisher made, and the artifact should say so on every run rather than let a dead series look alive.

series.detail: local_policy_rate: last observation 2026-06-01 is 95 days behind the run date, tolerance is 75 (monthly, published in arrears)

tolerance.rationale: The immediate-rate series runs a full month or more behind: on the 2026-08-12 read its last observation was 2026-05. Seventy-five days is set from that observed lag rather than from the monthly calendar alone, which would fire on every ordinary run.

series.detail: real_yield_10y: last observation 2026-09-02 is 2 days behind the run date, tolerance is 5 (US business days)

tolerance.rationale: DFII10 is published each business day with about a one-day lag. Five days absorbs a Monday holiday landing on top of that lag.

series.detail: usdinr: last observation 2026-09-04 is 0 days behind the run date, tolerance is 4 (FX trading days)

tolerance.rationale: FX trades Sunday 22:00 to Friday 22:00 UTC, so the calendar matches the fix's. Blocking because the rupee lens converts through it: a stale rate over a fresh fix publishes a rupee price that was never quoted.

series.detail: vix: last observation 2026-09-02 is 2 days behind the run date, tolerance is 5 (US equity market days)

tolerance.rationale: Yahoo carries the previous session by the following morning; the FRED fallback lags a day further. Five days covers a long weekend plus the fallback's own lag without hiding a genuine multi-day outage.

series.detail: wti: last observation 2026-09-01 is 3 days behind the run date, tolerance is 7 (US business days, published in arrears)

tolerance.calendar: US business days, published in arrears
tolerance.rationale: DCOILWTICO was three days behind on the 2026-07-30 run. Seven days covers that lag plus a holiday week.

series.detail: xau_futures: last observation 2026-09-04 is 0 days behind the run date, tolerance is 4 (COMEX trading days)

tolerance.rationale: Not blocking — futures feed the realised-volatility estimators, never a published price. Declared and measured anyway so a Yahoo rate limit that silently degrades the vol layer to close-only is visible in the artifact.

series.detail: xauusd: last observation 2026-09-03 is 1 days behind the run date, tolerance is 4 (London business days (LBMA PM fix))

tolerance.rationale: The PM fix prints at 15:00 London, so it is available well before a 02:00 UTC run the next day. The longest ordinary gap is a 02:00 Tuesday run after a Monday holiday reading Friday's fix — four days. Anything beyond that is a multi-day closure or a broken source, and both must refuse: this series is the anchor every published price and every simulated path is built from.

policy_breaks.description: Gold import duty moves from specific (Rs 300/10g) to 2% ad valorem.
Duty to 10% alongside the 80:20 rule requiring 20% of imports be re-exported. The quantitative restriction, more than the duty, drove the very large domestic premia of 2013-2014.
80:20 import-linkage rule withdrawn; domestic premia normalise.
Demonetisation. Cash-market disruption produced a sharp, temporary dislocation between official and effective retail gold pricing.
GST replaces state VAT and excise. Start of the nationally-comparable parity regime.
Duty restructured to BCD 7.5% + AIDC 2.5%; total payable falls to 10%.
Duty cut to 6% (BCD 5% + AIDC 1%), lowest in over a decade.
Duty raised to 15% (BCD 10% + AIDC 5%) via Notifications 15-18/2026-Customs.
